screens.title: Anatomy of a Basic Chaincode
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will unpack a minimal Hyperledger Fabric chaincode written in Go, using the common asset transfer example to ground each idea. You will learn why the program begins with package main, what the main function actually does for chaincode, and how contractapi. NewChaincode and Start prepare your contract to listen for peer invocations. We will examine the SmartContract struct and why embedding contractapi. Contract matters, and you will see how transaction methods use a transaction context interface to call GetState, PutState and DelState on the world state. We'll also define an Asset struct and show how marshaling to JSON bytes and unmarshaling back to Go structs is the practical bridge between code and ledger storage. Along the way I will point out common mistakes such as forgetting error checks, mismatched JSON tags, and non-idempotent operations. By the end you will be able to read a small myasset. go file and explain each piece: initialization, contract wiring, the ledger stub, structured assets, and safe write/read patterns. Keep an eye out for the InitLedger example — it shows how to seed assets reliably and why JSON tags matter for consistent marshaling.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A Go chaincode is an executable whose main function initializes a SmartContract that embeds contractapi.Contract and starts a chaincode server; assets are stored as JSON byte arrays via the ledger stub.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Anatomy of a Basic Chaincode
Anatomy of a Basic Chaincode
A compact walkthrough of how a Go chaincode is structured, initialized, and how it manages assets on the ledger.
In this lesson
Entry point, contract wiring, and the ledger stub.
Coming up
SmartContract structure and JSON marshaling.
Hands-on
InitLedger example to seed the world state.
Code-first view
Topic: Entry
package main and the main function initialize the chaincode server.
Topic: Contract
SmartContract embeds contractapi.Contract so Fabric recognizes your methods.
Topic: Assets
Assets are Go structs marshaled to JSON bytes for world state storage.
Visual concept
Chaincode wiring
A SmartContract type is created, wrapped by contractapi, and started so the peer can invoke its transaction methods.
package main

func main() {
  chaincode, err := contractapi.NewChaincode(&SmartContract{})
  if err != nil { log.Panicf("Error creating chaincode: %v", err) }

  if err := chaincode.Start(); err != nil { log.Panicf("Error starting chaincode: %v", err) }
}
Key Takeaway

The main function wires your SmartContract into the Fabric runtime; business logic belongs inside methods on that struct.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In these objectives we set clear, verifiable outcomes so you can measure progress. First, you will deconstruct the standard layout of a Go chaincode project. That means identifying package main, imports, the SmartContract type, and the main function that starts the chaincode server. As you practice, this helps you quickly assess new chaincode examples. Second, you'll explain the role of the main function and the pair contractapi. NewChaincode plus chaincode. Start. Practically, this explains how Fabric hands transaction invocations to your code. Third, you will understand why SmartContract must embed contractapi. Contract so it gains access to transaction context and ledger stubs. This is essential for your methods to be invoked correctly. Fourth, you will differentiate transaction functions that read from versus write to the world state, and why marshaling and unmarshaling JSON bytes matters to that difference. Each objective maps to a small competency: read a myasset. go file, explain main and Start, identify embedding and transaction context, and classify methods as reads or writes. Achieving these objectives prepares you to implement InitLedger and safe PutState/GetState calls.

screens.title: package main and the executable entry point
screens.narratorSegment: Start by recognizing that every Go chaincode file begins with package main because the chaincode is an executable program run inside a container. package main signals to the Go toolchain that the package should compile to an executable binary, which the Fabric peer loads into a chaincode container. The entry point for that executable is the main function. Unlike a typical command-line program whose main might orchestrate business logic or CLI parsing, a chaincode main function has a narrower responsibility: initialize and start the chaincode runtime so it can receive transaction requests from the peer. Concretely, main constructs your SmartContract implementation and hands it to contractapi. NewChaincode, which wraps the implementation into a runnable chaincode object. Then main calls Start on that wrapped object to begin listening. An important practical point: treat main as wiring code rather than business logic. Put operational initialization, logging setup, or feature flags there, but never embed core transaction behavior in main. This separation keeps unit tests focused on the SmartContract methods and ensures the runtime wiring is minimal and auditable. One common misconception is thinking package main implies the code will run like a desktop app; instead it becomes a server that responds to transactional invocations. For practice, inspect a myasset. go file and find package main, the imports, and the concise main function: that small function is what turns your contract code into a Fabric-managed executable.

keyIdea.title: Why package main matters
keyIdea.text: It marks the code as an executable entrypoint so the Fabric peer can run the chaincode container and invoke your SmartContract methods.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › package main
package main: the executable
Declare the package as an executable so the Go compiler produces a runnable binary used by the peer.
Why this matters
  • Signals an executable program rather than a library.
  • Main function becomes the chaincode wiring point, not business logic.
  • Keeps runtime concerns separated from transaction methods for testability.
Common misconception
Do not place transaction logic in main. Main should only set up and start the chaincode server.
Code snapshot
package main

func main() {
  chaincode, err := contractapi.NewChaincode(&SmartContract{})
  if err != nil { log.Panicf("Error creating myasset chaincode: %v", err) }

  if err := chaincode.Start(); err != nil { log.Panicf("Error starting myasset chaincode: %v", err) }
}
Key Takeaway

Main wires your contract into the Fabric runtime; keep it minimal so your contract methods stay testable.

screens.title: contractapi.NewChaincode and chaincode.Start
screens.narratorSegment: When your chaincode runs inside a Fabric peer, it doesn't magically know how to accept transactions — your code must be wrapped by the Contract A P I. The function contractapi. NewChaincode takes a pointer to your SmartContract implementation and returns a chaincode object that conforms to the Fabric runtime's expectations. This wrapper inspects exported methods on the struct and registers them so the peer can invoke them by name. After wrapping, calling Start begins the listening loop: the chaincode process will accept requests from the peer, decode arguments, and dispatch to the corresponding method on your SmartContract. Think of NewChaincode as registration and Start as the server loop. A useful mental model is a small web server: NewChaincode maps routes to handler functions, and Start begins accepting requests. One common pitfall is failing to check errors returned by NewChaincode or Start. If NewChaincode returns an error, your contract is not registered correctly; if Start fails, the chaincode container does not enter the ready state and the peer cannot route transactions to it. For hands-on verification, run the chaincode and watch logs for successful initialization messages. Misunderstanding this wiring leads learners to look for business logic in the wrong place; remember, transaction logic lives on methods of SmartContract, not inside Start.

keyIdea.title: Registration vs listening
keyIdea.text: NewChaincode registers your contract implementation; Start begins listening for peer-invoked transactions and dispatches to your methods.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › NewChaincode & Start
How it works
Registration and listening are distinct steps that make your SmartContract reachable by the Fabric peer.
Step 1
NewChaincode wraps your implementation and inspects exported methods.
Step 2
Start begins the server loop to receive and dispatch peer invocations.
  • NewChaincode maps names to methods so invocation works by function name.
  • Start must succeed for the chaincode to be ready; always handle errors.
  • Think of this as registering routes and starting a tiny RPC server.
Common mistake
Ignoring errors from NewChaincode or Start will leave your chaincode unreachable and hard to debug.
Quick check example
chaincode, err := contractapi.NewChaincode(&SmartContract{})
if err != nil { log.Panicf("Error creating chaincode: %v", err) }

if err := chaincode.Start(); err != nil { log.Panicf("Error starting chaincode: %v", err) }
Key Takeaway

Treat NewChaincode as registration and Start as activation; always check and handle returned errors.

screens.title: SmartContract struct and embedding contractapi.Contract
screens.narratorSegment: At the heart of your chaincode lies the SmartContract struct. It is the container for all transaction methods that implement your business logic. A crucial detail is that your SmartContract must embed contractapi. Contract. Embedding gives your struct the behaviors and interfaces the Fabric Contract A P I expects, including the ability to receive a TransactionContextInterface when a method is invoked. The TransactionContextInterface contains the stub that exposes PutState, GetState and DelState and also carries transaction metadata. Embedding is not magic: it simply composes the helper behavior into your type so the framework recognizes it. Without embedding, your methods won't be bound correctly and the Contract A P I will not expose the context the way it expects. From an architecture perspective, treat your SmartContract as the public surface — exported methods become callable transactions. Keep the struct lightweight: only fields that represent shared helper objects or configuration should be placed there; avoid storing transient per-transaction data as struct fields. A common confusion is thinking embedding adds fields automatically; instead it enables method and interface matching so the Contract A P I can wire the context and call your functions. In practice, implement methods with the signature that accepts ctx contractapi. TransactionContextInterface and rely on ctx. GetStub() to interact with the ledger. That keeps concerns separated and testability high.

keyIdea.title: Embedding provides integration
keyIdea.text: Embedding contractapi.Contract lets the Fabric Contract API recognize your type and supply a TransactionContextInterface to each transaction method.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › SmartContract & Embedding
SmartContract structure
Define a struct that embeds contractapi.Contract so your methods receive a proper context.
// SmartContract provides functions for managing an Asset
type SmartContract struct {
  contractapi.Contract
}
  • Embedding composes contractapi functionality into your type.
  • Transaction methods accept ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface.
  • Keep SmartContract lightweight to preserve testability.
Practical notes
Use ctx.GetStub() for all ledger operations and avoid storing per-transaction state on the struct itself.
Pitfall
If you forget to embed contractapi.Contract, methods may not be recognized or receive the correct context; embedding is required for proper invocation.
Key Takeaway

Embedding connects your struct to the Contract API, enabling context, stub access, and method registration.

screens.title: TransactionContextInterface and the ledger stub
screens.narratorSegment: Every transaction method receives a context value, typically named ctx, that implements the TransactionContextInterface. This interface is the gateway to ledger operations and transaction metadata. The most important function on ctx is GetStub, which yields the ChaincodeStubInterface. The stub provides low-level methods such as PutState, GetState and DelState that operate on key-value pairs in the world state. It's important to remember these functions work with byte arrays, so you must marshal structured data into JSON bytes before writing and unmarshal after reading. Use the stub to emit events and to access transient data or query chaincode state. A misconception to avoid is thinking ctx itself stores state; ctx is a transient per-transaction interface that exposes operations via the stub. From a safety perspective, always check for and return errors from stub calls because network or serialization issues can cause PutState or GetState to fail. For example, GetState returns nil and no error if the key doesn't exist; so check returned bytes before unmarshaling. Also prefer idempotent writes where possible: if a function can be safely retried without side effects, it reduces errors when clients retry transactions. Practically, your method signatures look like func (s *SmartContract) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi. TransactionContextInterface,...) error and you use ctx. GetStub(). PutState to persist data.

keyIdea.title: Context is your gateway
keyIdea.text: Use ctx.GetStub() to access the ledger stub; all world state operations are byte-array based and can return errors you must check.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Transaction Context
TransactionContextInterface
ctx supplies GetStub and access to transaction metadata so each method can interact with the ledger safely.
  • Use ctx.GetStub() to obtain PutState, GetState, DelState.
  • All PutState/GetState work with byte arrays; marshal and unmarshal accordingly.
  • Check for nil returns and errors from GetState before unmarshaling.
Quick examples
// write
err = ctx.GetStub().PutState(asset.ID, assetJSON)
if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to put to world state: %v", err) }

// read
assetBytes, err := ctx.GetStub().GetState(assetID)
if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to read from world state: %v", err) }
if assetBytes == nil { return fmt.Errorf("asset not found: %s", assetID) }
Pro tip
Always validate returned bytes and errors from GetState to avoid panics during unmarshaling.

screens.title: Assets as structured data
screens.narratorSegment: An Asset represents a real-world or digital entity whose state you store on the ledger. In the asset transfer example the Asset struct includes fields like ID, Color, Size, Owner, and AppraisedValue. Crucially, each field carries a json:"..." struct tag. Those tags instruct the encoding/json package how to map Go fields to JSON object keys when marshaling and unmarshaling. For example, a field declared as ID string json. "ID" will produce or expect a JSON key named ID. If tags are missing or incorrect, marshaling may produce unexpected keys or omit fields entirely, leading to silent failures when reading data later. Always keep your struct definition consistent across methods that use the same data shape. When you marshal an Asset with json. Marshal, you get a byte slice suitable for PutState. When reading, GetState returns bytes that you must json. Unmarshal into the same Asset type. A common mistake is attempting to unmarshal into a different struct shape; that often fails quietly or sets zero values. For robustness, check for errors after marshaling and unmarshaling and validate required fields after reading from the ledger. Structuring assets this way keeps ledger data predictable and interoperable between different chaincode versions or client applications.

keyIdea.title: Structured assets
keyIdea.text: Define assets with explicit JSON tags so marshaling produces predictable keys and unmarshaling reconstructs the original object reliably.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Asset struct
Asset struct example
Fields and JSON tags control how the struct appears in stored JSON bytes.
type Asset struct {
  ID             string `json:"ID"`
  Color          string `json:"color"`
  Size           int    `json:"size"`
  Owner          string `json:"owner"`
  AppraisedValue int    `json:"appraisedValue"`
}
  • JSON tags define exact key names for marshaling and unmarshaling.
  • Consistency across methods prevents silent data mismatches.
  • Validate fields after unmarshaling to catch corrupt or unexpected data.
Why tags matter
Tags are the contract between your chaincode and the JSON representation stored on the ledger; changing them is a breaking change unless you handle migration.
Common mistake
Omitting json tags or changing key names leads to failing unmarshals or missing fields when clients expect a stable shape.
Key Takeaway

Design your Asset struct and tags deliberately; treat the JSON shape as part of your chaincode's public interface.

screens.title: InitLedger: seeding the world state
screens.narratorSegment: InitLedger provides a concrete example of using marshaling and PutState to initialize the ledger with sample data. The function constructs a slice of Asset values, iterates through them, marshals each asset to JSON bytes, then calls ctx. GetStub(). PutState with the asset ID and bytes. Each step must check errors: json. Marshal can fail if a field contains unsupported types, and PutState can fail for stub or network issues. Logging during initialization is useful for visibility but don't rely on logs for correctness. Note that InitLedger is typically called only once, at chaincode instantiation or commit, so it should idempotently handle repeated calls or detect preexisting keys if needed. For example, the sample code creates four assets with distinct IDs, marshals each, checks for marshal errors, and returns formatted errors if PutState fails. A practical tip: after writing your InitLedger, use a test or a lightweight script to call it and then ReadAsset for each ID to ensure the stored JSON unmarshals back into the expected Asset struct. A misconception is assuming PutState stores typed objects; it only stores bytes. The struct-to-bytes and bytes-to-struct transitions are explicit and require json tags to match. In short, InitLedger shows the full pipeline from Go struct to persistent ledger entry and back again.

keyIdea.title: InitLedger pipeline
keyIdea.text: Create assets, marshal to JSON bytes, use PutState to persist, and always check errors; test by reading back and unmarshaling.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › InitLedger
InitLedger example
Create a list of assets, marshal each to JSON, and PutState to persist them.
func (s *SmartContract) InitLedger(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface) error {
  assets := []Asset{
    {ID: "asset1", Color: "blue", Size: 5, Owner: "Tomoko", AppraisedValue: 300},
    {ID: "asset2", Color: "red", Size: 5, Owner: "Brad", AppraisedValue: 400},
    {ID: "asset3", Color: "green", Size: 10, Owner: "Jin", AppraisedValue: 500},
    {ID: "asset4", Color: "yellow", Size: 10, Owner: "Max", AppraisedValue: 600},
  }

  for _, asset := range assets {
    assetJSON, err := json.Marshal(asset)
    if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to marshal asset %s: %v", asset.ID, err) }

    err = ctx.GetStub().PutState(asset.ID, assetJSON)
    if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to put to world state. %v", err) }
  }

  return nil
}
Checks and balances
Always handle marshal and PutState errors. Consider pre-checking for existing keys if InitLedger may run more than once.
Practical test
Call InitLedger, then call ReadAsset for each ID and unmarshal the returned bytes to validate the stored shape and values.
Key Takeaway

InitLedger demonstrates the end-to-end flow: struct → JSON bytes → PutState → GetState → struct.

screens.title: CreateAsset and ReadAsset: write and read patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Transaction methods usually fall into two categories: writes that change the world state and reads that return data. CreateAsset is a typical write method: it accepts parameters such as assetID, color, size, owner, and appraisedValue; constructs an Asset struct; marshals it to JSON bytes; and calls ctx. GetStub(). PutState with the bytes. Always check for errors at each step. A common safety improvement is to check whether an asset with the same ID already exists to avoid accidental overwrites. ReadAsset is a read method: it calls ctx. GetStub(). GetState, checks the returned bytes and error, and then unmarshals into an Asset struct. If GetState returns nil, that indicates the key wasn't found and your method should return a clear error. Remember that reads can be either query-only or part of a larger transaction; therefore design read methods to be side-effect free. A frequent misconception is thinking GetState returns typed structs — it returns bytes. You must convert those bytes back into the expected type with json. Unmarshal. For maintainability, keep input validation, error handling, and marshaling responsibilities explicit and consistent across create, update, and read methods. This pattern makes your chaincode predictable and easier to debug when clients interact with it.

keyIdea.title: Read vs write
keyIdea.text: Writes marshal structs to bytes and PutState them; reads GetState bytes and unmarshal to structs. Validate existence and errors at every step.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › CreateAsset & ReadAsset
CreateAsset (write)
Construct a struct, marshal to JSON bytes, and PutState with the asset ID.
func (s *SmartContract) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, assetID string, color string, size int, owner string, appraisedValue int) error {
  asset := Asset{ID: assetID, Color: color, Size: size, Owner: owner, AppraisedValue: appraisedValue}
  assetJSON, err := json.Marshal(asset)
  if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to marshal asset: %v", err) }

  return ctx.GetStub().PutState(assetID, assetJSON)
}
ReadAsset (read)
GetState returns bytes; check for nil and unmarshal into the Asset struct.
func (s *SmartContract) ReadAsset(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, assetID string) (*Asset, error) {
  assetBytes, err := ctx.GetStub().GetState(assetID)
  if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to read from world state: %v", err) }
  if assetBytes == nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("asset not found: %s", assetID) }

  var asset Asset
  if err := json.Unmarshal(assetBytes, &asset); err != nil { return nil, err }
  return &asset, nil
}
Key Takeaway

Treat writes and reads symmetrically: explicit marshal before PutState and explicit unmarshal after GetState, with clear existence checks.

screens.title: Marshaling vs Unmarshaling
screens.narratorSegment: Marshaling and unmarshaling are the explicit conversions you perform when moving data between your Go types and the ledger. Marshaling uses json. Marshal to convert a struct into a JSON byte slice suitable for PutState. Unmarshaling uses json. Unmarshal to convert bytes returned from GetState into a struct. The most critical requirement is symmetry: the struct shape and JSON tags used during marshaling must match the type you unmarshal into. If they differ, you'll get missing fields or zero values, and sometimes an error. Also remember that json. Marshal can fail if a field contains unsupported values like channels or functions. After unmarshaling verify required fields are present — for example, ensure ID or Owner is non-empty — because the ledger may have been written by a different client or an older contract version. Another common misunderstanding is relying on default JSON field names when tags are present; tags override defaults. Additionally, consider backward compatibility: if you change the struct or tags in a new chaincode version, plan a migration so older stored JSON still unmarshals correctly. Finally, always handle and propagate errors from both json. Marshal and json. Unmarshal; silent failures lead to confusing runtime behavior. A brief practical exercise is to marshal an Asset, store and read it, then intentionally change a tag to observe the effect during unmarshaling.

Marshaling
Convert Asset struct to JSON bytes before writing.
assetJSON, err := json.Marshal(asset)
if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("failed to marshal asset %s: %v", asset.ID, err) }
  • Tags control JSON key names.

if err := json.Unmarshal(assetBytes, &asset); err != nil { return nil, err }

Try this

screens.title: Error handling and idempotency
screens.narratorSegment: Robust chaincode depends on careful error handling and idempotent design. Every call that interacts with the stub or performs marshaling can fail and should return an error that the Fabric runtime and client can observe. For example, json. Marshal might return an error on unsupported types, and ctx. GetStub(). PutState can fail due to stub or network problems. Always check errors immediately and return descriptive messages. Idempotency means that re-executing a function with the same input should have the same effect as executing it once. For writes, this often means first checking for the existence of a key and deciding whether to reject duplicates or treat a create as a no-op. For updates, ensure that repeated calls do not corrupt data or cause unintended side effects. Idempotency simplifies recovery from retries and transient failures in distributed systems. Another defensive pattern is explicit validation after unmarshaling: verify required fields, value ranges, and types. Logging is helpful during development and troubleshooting, but do not rely on logs for program correctness. A common misconception is to implement all error handling only at the top-level; instead, handle and wrap errors close to their source so callers get context-rich messages. By combining careful error checks, consistent marshaling, and idempotent operations, your chaincode becomes predictable and resilient under retries and partial failures.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will unpack a minimal Hyperledger Fabric chaincode written in Go, using the common asset transfer example to ground each idea. You will learn why the program begins with package main, what the main function actually does for chaincode, and how contractapi. NewChaincode and Start prepare your contract to listen for peer invocations. We will examine the SmartContract struct and why embedding contractapi. Contract matters, and you will see how transaction methods use a transaction context interface to call GetState, PutState and DelState on the world state. We'll also define an Asset struct and show how marshaling to JSON bytes and unmarshaling back to Go structs is the practical bridge between code and ledger storage. Along the way I will point out common mistakes such as forgetting error checks, mismatched JSON tags, and non-idempotent operations. By the end you will be able to read a small myasset. go file and explain each piece: initialization, contract wiring, the ledger stub, structured assets, and safe write/read patterns. Keep an eye out for the InitLedger example — it shows how to seed assets reliably and why JSON tags matter for consistent marshaling.

In these objectives we set clear, verifiable outcomes so you can measure progress. First, you will deconstruct the standard layout of a Go chaincode project. That means identifying package main, imports, the SmartContract type, and the main function that starts the chaincode server. As you practice, this helps you quickly assess new chaincode examples. Second, you'll explain the role of the main function and the pair contractapi. NewChaincode plus chaincode. Start. Practically, this explains how Fabric hands transaction invocations to your code. Third, you will understand why SmartContract must embed contractapi. Contract so it gains access to transaction context and ledger stubs. This is essential for your methods to be invoked correctly. Fourth, you will differentiate transaction functions that read from versus write to the world state, and why marshaling and unmarshaling JSON bytes matters to that difference. Each objective maps to a small competency: read a myasset. go file, explain main and Start, identify embedding and transaction context, and classify methods as reads or writes. Achieving these objectives prepares you to implement InitLedger and safe PutState/GetState calls.

This second objectives slide emphasizes doing and verifying. One objective reinforces reading a myasset. go file and mapping each section to runtime behavior, which helps during code reviews and debugging. Another objective asks you to explain contractapi. NewChaincode and chaincode. Start in terms of how the peer delivers transaction requests to your contract implementation. The third objective focuses on making SmartContract methods accessible by embedding contractapi. Contract and using the TransactionContextInterface; this gives access to the stub for ledger operations and transaction metadata. The fourth objective highlights marshaling and unmarshaling: you must be able to convert an Asset struct to JSON bytes before storing it and reverse the process when reading. Practically, these skills let you implement InitLedger, CreateAsset, and ReadAsset safely. For each objective you should be able to show a one-minute demo or short unit test that demonstrates the competency. Think of these objectives as small, verifiable milestones on your path to writing robust, predictable chaincode.

Start by recognizing that every Go chaincode file begins with package main because the chaincode is an executable program run inside a container. package main signals to the Go toolchain that the package should compile to an executable binary, which the Fabric peer loads into a chaincode container. The entry point for that executable is the main function. Unlike a typical command-line program whose main might orchestrate business logic or CLI parsing, a chaincode main function has a narrower responsibility: initialize and start the chaincode runtime so it can receive transaction requests from the peer. Concretely, main constructs your SmartContract implementation and hands it to contractapi. NewChaincode, which wraps the implementation into a runnable chaincode object. Then main calls Start on that wrapped object to begin listening. An important practical point: treat main as wiring code rather than business logic. Put operational initialization, logging setup, or feature flags there, but never embed core transaction behavior in main. This separation keeps unit tests focused on the SmartContract methods and ensures the runtime wiring is minimal and auditable. One common misconception is thinking package main implies the code will run like a desktop app; instead it becomes a server that responds to transactional invocations. For practice, inspect a myasset. go file and find package main, the imports, and the concise main function: that small function is what turns your contract code into a Fabric-managed executable.

When your chaincode runs inside a Fabric peer, it doesn't magically know how to accept transactions — your code must be wrapped by the Contract A P I. The function contractapi. NewChaincode takes a pointer to your SmartContract implementation and returns a chaincode object that conforms to the Fabric runtime's expectations. This wrapper inspects exported methods on the struct and registers them so the peer can invoke them by name. After wrapping, calling Start begins the listening loop: the chaincode process will accept requests from the peer, decode arguments, and dispatch to the corresponding method on your SmartContract. Think of NewChaincode as registration and Start as the server loop. A useful mental model is a small web server: NewChaincode maps routes to handler functions, and Start begins accepting requests. One common pitfall is failing to check errors returned by NewChaincode or Start. If NewChaincode returns an error, your contract is not registered correctly; if Start fails, the chaincode container does not enter the ready state and the peer cannot route transactions to it. For hands-on verification, run the chaincode and watch logs for successful initialization messages. Misunderstanding this wiring leads learners to look for business logic in the wrong place; remember, transaction logic lives on methods of SmartContract, not inside Start.

At the heart of your chaincode lies the SmartContract struct. It is the container for all transaction methods that implement your business logic. A crucial detail is that your SmartContract must embed contractapi. Contract. Embedding gives your struct the behaviors and interfaces the Fabric Contract A P I expects, including the ability to receive a TransactionContextInterface when a method is invoked. The TransactionContextInterface contains the stub that exposes PutState, GetState and DelState and also carries transaction metadata. Embedding is not magic: it simply composes the helper behavior into your type so the framework recognizes it. Without embedding, your methods won't be bound correctly and the Contract A P I will not expose the context the way it expects. From an architecture perspective, treat your SmartContract as the public surface — exported methods become callable transactions. Keep the struct lightweight: only fields that represent shared helper objects or configuration should be placed there; avoid storing transient per-transaction data as struct fields. A common confusion is thinking embedding adds fields automatically; instead it enables method and interface matching so the Contract A P I can wire the context and call your functions. In practice, implement methods with the signature that accepts ctx contractapi. TransactionContextInterface and rely on ctx. GetStub() to interact with the ledger. That keeps concerns separated and testability high.

Every transaction method receives a context value, typically named ctx, that implements the TransactionContextInterface. This interface is the gateway to ledger operations and transaction metadata. The most important function on ctx is GetStub, which yields the ChaincodeStubInterface. The stub provides low-level methods such as PutState, GetState and DelState that operate on key-value pairs in the world state. It's important to remember these functions work with byte arrays, so you must marshal structured data into JSON bytes before writing and unmarshal after reading. Use the stub to emit events and to access transient data or query chaincode state. A misconception to avoid is thinking ctx itself stores state; ctx is a transient per-transaction interface that exposes operations via the stub. From a safety perspective, always check for and return errors from stub calls because network or serialization issues can cause PutState or GetState to fail. For example, GetState returns nil and no error if the key doesn't exist; so check returned bytes before unmarshaling. Also prefer idempotent writes where possible: if a function can be safely retried without side effects, it reduces errors when clients retry transactions. Practically, your method signatures look like func (s *SmartContract) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi. TransactionContextInterface,...) error and you use ctx. GetStub(). PutState to persist data.

An Asset represents a real-world or digital entity whose state you store on the ledger. In the asset transfer example the Asset struct includes fields like ID, Color, Size, Owner, and AppraisedValue. Crucially, each field carries a json:"..." struct tag. Those tags instruct the encoding/json package how to map Go fields to JSON object keys when marshaling and unmarshaling. For example, a field declared as ID string json. "ID" will produce or expect a JSON key named ID. If tags are missing or incorrect, marshaling may produce unexpected keys or omit fields entirely, leading to silent failures when reading data later. Always keep your struct definition consistent across methods that use the same data shape. When you marshal an Asset with json. Marshal, you get a byte slice suitable for PutState. When reading, GetState returns bytes that you must json. Unmarshal into the same Asset type. A common mistake is attempting to unmarshal into a different struct shape; that often fails quietly or sets zero values. For robustness, check for errors after marshaling and unmarshaling and validate required fields after reading from the ledger. Structuring assets this way keeps ledger data predictable and interoperable between different chaincode versions or client applications.

InitLedger provides a concrete example of using marshaling and PutState to initialize the ledger with sample data. The function constructs a slice of Asset values, iterates through them, marshals each asset to JSON bytes, then calls ctx. GetStub(). PutState with the asset ID and bytes. Each step must check errors: json. Marshal can fail if a field contains unsupported types, and PutState can fail for stub or network issues. Logging during initialization is useful for visibility but don't rely on logs for correctness. Note that InitLedger is typically called only once, at chaincode instantiation or commit, so it should idempotently handle repeated calls or detect preexisting keys if needed. For example, the sample code creates four assets with distinct IDs, marshals each, checks for marshal errors, and returns formatted errors if PutState fails. A practical tip: after writing your InitLedger, use a test or a lightweight script to call it and then ReadAsset for each ID to ensure the stored JSON unmarshals back into the expected Asset struct. A misconception is assuming PutState stores typed objects; it only stores bytes. The struct-to-bytes and bytes-to-struct transitions are explicit and require json tags to match. In short, InitLedger shows the full pipeline from Go struct to persistent ledger entry and back again.

Transaction methods usually fall into two categories: writes that change the world state and reads that return data. CreateAsset is a typical write method: it accepts parameters such as assetID, color, size, owner, and appraisedValue; constructs an Asset struct; marshals it to JSON bytes; and calls ctx. GetStub(). PutState with the bytes. Always check for errors at each step. A common safety improvement is to check whether an asset with the same ID already exists to avoid accidental overwrites. ReadAsset is a read method: it calls ctx. GetStub(). GetState, checks the returned bytes and error, and then unmarshals into an Asset struct. If GetState returns nil, that indicates the key wasn't found and your method should return a clear error. Remember that reads can be either query-only or part of a larger transaction; therefore design read methods to be side-effect free. A frequent misconception is thinking GetState returns typed structs — it returns bytes. You must convert those bytes back into the expected type with json. Unmarshal. For maintainability, keep input validation, error handling, and marshaling responsibilities explicit and consistent across create, update, and read methods. This pattern makes your chaincode predictable and easier to debug when clients interact with it.

Marshaling and unmarshaling are the explicit conversions you perform when moving data between your Go types and the ledger. Marshaling uses json. Marshal to convert a struct into a JSON byte slice suitable for PutState. Unmarshaling uses json. Unmarshal to convert bytes returned from GetState into a struct. The most critical requirement is symmetry: the struct shape and JSON tags used during marshaling must match the type you unmarshal into. If they differ, you'll get missing fields or zero values, and sometimes an error. Also remember that json. Marshal can fail if a field contains unsupported values like channels or functions. After unmarshaling verify required fields are present — for example, ensure ID or Owner is non-empty — because the ledger may have been written by a different client or an older contract version. Another common misunderstanding is relying on default JSON field names when tags are present; tags override defaults. Additionally, consider backward compatibility: if you change the struct or tags in a new chaincode version, plan a migration so older stored JSON still unmarshals correctly. Finally, always handle and propagate errors from both json. Marshal and json. Unmarshal; silent failures lead to confusing runtime behavior. A brief practical exercise is to marshal an Asset, store and read it, then intentionally change a tag to observe the effect during unmarshaling.

Robust chaincode depends on careful error handling and idempotent design. Every call that interacts with the stub or performs marshaling can fail and should return an error that the Fabric runtime and client can observe. For example, json. Marshal might return an error on unsupported types, and ctx. GetStub(). PutState can fail due to stub or network problems. Always check errors immediately and return descriptive messages. Idempotency means that re-executing a function with the same input should have the same effect as executing it once. For writes, this often means first checking for the existence of a key and deciding whether to reject duplicates or treat a create as a no-op. For updates, ensure that repeated calls do not corrupt data or cause unintended side effects. Idempotency simplifies recovery from retries and transient failures in distributed systems. Another defensive pattern is explicit validation after unmarshaling: verify required fields, value ranges, and types. Logging is helpful during development and troubleshooting, but do not rely on logs for program correctness. A common misconception is to implement all error handling only at the top-level; instead, handle and wrap errors close to their source so callers get context-rich messages. By combining careful error checks, consistent marshaling, and idempotent operations, your chaincode becomes predictable and resilient under retries and partial failures.
